Q: Gunicorn with Flask using wrong Python A:

Assuming your virtual environment is called env, your application is called app, and Gunicorn is installed properly, you may try:

sudo env/bin/gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:5432 wsgi:app

This forces the application to use the Gunicorn in your virtual environment.

Q: SQL Select from a table where the column name is a value in the table A:

See simple example with NULLIF and COALESCE

SELECT sector,program, 
   COALESCE(nullif(CA1,N''),nullif(CA2,N''),nullif(CA3,N'')) as control_account,
   COALESCE(nullif(CA1_DESC,N''),nullif(CA2_DESC,N''),nullif(CA3_DESC,N'')) as control_account_desc,
   [WP], [DESCRIP]
FROM WF1_DATA;

Q: Is it safe to auto-generate Alembic migrations in CI/CD pipeline for a shared database? A:

The application connects to a shared AWS-hosted database for development.

Do you need to? This leads to all sorts of potential trouble. You highlight a couple of them:

How does this approach handle concurrent changes (e.g., multiple branches modifying models)?

Really badly. Consider a setup where Anna and Bill are working together on a project, and

  1. Anna adds a migration to add column A to table X, and test deploys it on her branch.
  2. Bill adds columns A and B to table X, and test deploys it on his branch. Column A already exists in the database, so the migration only adds column B.
  3. Anna and Bill talk in their daily standup and realize their work overlaps, so Anna deletes her branch.

Now the shared database still has column A (Anna never ran her down migration) so all of Bill's tests still pass. But now in other environments nothing introduces column A at all, and this change (which has been locally tested and code reviewed) fails when it reaches the pre-production environment. Now it needs to be reverted, and the release manager is frustrated that they need to manually run a down migration as part of a revert.

Most projects I've worked on have the ability to set up a local database for development. The most common approach starts from an empty database, runs all of the (up) migrations, and possibly runs a seed-data job to add data to it. The best approach IME is able to use an in-memory SQLite database, so you can get a lightweight clean database, even per-test if needed.

In a previous role, we maintained a reference set of database dumps that developers could import into their local databases. This could be helpful if the required seed data is substantial. It was also a regular source of trouble where a developer started from a week-old data dump, since downloading and reloading the data was somewhat expensive.

Q: Understand how caching helps in auto-refreshing Superset dashboards A:

I'm new to Superset and caching, but here's my understanding.

If a reader opens a report that has recently been cached, instead of the report being run again, a cached version is fetched from Redis. Redis can store and transmit data faster than a relational database - that's one advantage. This reduces traffic on the database as well.

The other advantage is that the cached report doesn't need to be re-computed, saving the need to run a potentially long-running and expensive query on your source database.

You can watch this happen by entering your Redis instance (for Docker, that means entering the container with docker exec -it superset_worker /bin/bash) and then running redis-cli. You can then run MONITOR to see all the transactions that are happening. And in the main Superset app, you can see when a report is fetched from the cache. Open those and then reload reports in your browser to generate the activity.

Your block of code would set up caching only of filters. You need similar blocks of code to set up filters for data, etc. Check the config.py file to see all the cache values that can be overwritten, then supply blocks of code similar to the one you have in your post for the other caches.

Here's a related post from Chartio, a Business Intelligence company that closed after being acquired, about the role of caching in serving their reports more efficiently.
